Automation of all sorts. Right now we're sort of stuck behind a dam. The thing holding that dam up was largely computer vision. Think about video games - the AI in even relatively simple games really dwarfs most of the automation today. Like a welding machine in a factory has no real concept of what it's doing and is minimal in the way of adjustments. It's just move 45 degrees down, weld for 1.3 seconds, move 45 degrees up, wait 3 seconds, go back to step 1. Computer vision is going to be an enormous game changer as it will allow AI systems to begin to actually grasp what they're doing. The same algorithm could then be changed to "Wait until a nonfinished strut is left in front of you. Weld each corner of that strut until bonded. Go back to step 1."

Pair that vision with comparably dramatic leaps in AI, or "brains", and the potential is far more than most realize. A recent proof of concept was AIs performing surgery. Unsurprisingly they were more precise than the best human surgeons. Pair that with the brains to understand what they're doing and the vision to be able to adjust on the fly and... yeah, we're not talking fast food self serve kiosks. Even in nonmechanical tasks other AI are already outperforming humans in diagnosing certain types of cancer. The really cool thing there is the AI that's talking about is Watson, the same AI that trounced humans on Jeopardy. The way it 'learned' to diagnose cancer was by autonomously consuming massive amounts of medical literature on the topic. The future is going to be... interesting.

Oh and another cool one is Mars. When Elon Musk talks about aiming to put people on Mars, and he's still sticking to a date of 2026, he's not talking about a few dozen scientists digging through the soil. He's talking about colonizing the planet - with hundreds of thousands of settlers aiming to produce a completely self sustaining colony and create a new entirely independent world.
